meta.name: Microsoft Azure Data Engineer Associate DP-203
meta.notes: [new pack: 12 authored DP-203 questions covering data storage design, data processing, data security, and optimization; answer positions balanced 3/3/3/3] [scheduled-agent]. v1.1: +10 — self-hosted IR, COPY INTO, SCD2, Delta time travel, session windows, medallion layers, Spark pool choice, tumbling window triggers, Event Hubs partition keys, failure alerting.

questions.question: You are loading a multi-terabyte sales fact table into a dedicated SQL pool in Azure Synapse Analytics. The table is almost always joined to large dimension tables on CustomerKey. Which table design minimizes data movement during those joins?
options: Hash-distribute the table on CustomerKey
Round-robin distribute the table
Replicate the table to every Compute node
Create the table as a heap with no clustered index
questions.explanation: Hash distribution on the join column (CustomerKey) co-locates matching rows on the same distribution, so joins on that key run without shuffling data between nodes. Round-robin spreads rows evenly but forces data movement on joins. Replicated tables are meant for small dimensions (roughly under 2 GB), not multi-terabyte facts. Heap versus clustered index controls storage and indexing, not distribution, so it does not address join data movement.

questions.question: A 50 MB product dimension table in a dedicated SQL pool is joined to many large fact tables. You want each Compute node to hold a full local copy so joins avoid shuffling the table at query time. Which distribution should you choose?
options: Hash distribution on ProductKey
Round-robin distribution
Replicated table
Partition the table by ProductCategory
questions.explanation: A replicated table stores a full copy on every Compute node, eliminating data movement for joins with small dimension tables (recommended for tables under about 2 GB). Hash and round-robin distributions split rows across distributions, so the table must be moved or shuffled at join time. Partitioning controls how rows are grouped for pruning and maintenance; it does not place a full copy on each node.

questions.question: You are provisioning an Azure Storage account that will serve as a data lake for Azure Synapse and Databricks, and you need directory-level POSIX ACLs plus atomic directory operations. Which option must you enable?
options: Geo-redundant storage (GRS)
The hierarchical namespace (Azure Data Lake Storage Gen2)
Soft delete for blobs
The Network File System (NFS) 3.0 protocol
questions.explanation: Enabling the hierarchical namespace turns a general-purpose v2 account into Azure Data Lake Storage Gen2, which adds true directories, atomic directory operations, and POSIX-style ACLs. GRS is a replication and redundancy setting. Soft delete protects against accidental deletion but adds no directory semantics. NFS 3.0 is a separate access protocol and is not what provides ACLs and directory structure for analytics.

questions.question: Queries against a large Parquet dataset in your data lake almost always filter by date. How should you organize the files so that a serverless SQL pool reads only the relevant data?
options: Store every file in a single flat container
Compress all files into one large ZIP archive per year
Name files sequentially (file001, file002, ...) with no folders
Store files in date-based folder partitions such as /year=2026/month=05/day=29/
questions.explanation: Partitioning the lake into date-based folders lets the engine apply partition elimination (pruning) using filepath() predicates, so only folders matching the date filter are scanned. A single flat container or sequential file names force a full scan. A ZIP archive is not a splittable analytical format and must be fully read and decompressed, defeating pruning.

questions.question: You need a file format for large analytical tables in the data lake that stores data by column, compresses well, and supports predicate and column pushdown for Spark and serverless SQL queries. Which format best fits?
options: Apache Parquet
Line-delimited JSON
CSV
Plain text logs
questions.explanation: Parquet is a columnar, compressed, self-describing format that supports column pruning and predicate pushdown, making it ideal for analytical queries in Spark and Synapse serverless SQL. JSON and CSV are row-oriented text formats that must be parsed in full and lack column statistics, so they scan far more data. Plain text logs are unstructured and even less efficient for analytics.

questions.question: You want to run ad-hoc T-SQL queries directly over Parquet files in Azure Data Lake Storage Gen2 without provisioning or paying for a running cluster, and be billed per terabyte of data processed. Which Azure Synapse capability should you use?
options: A dedicated SQL pool
An Apache Spark pool
The built-in serverless SQL pool with OPENROWSET
Azure Analysis Services
questions.explanation: The serverless SQL pool requires no provisioned infrastructure, is billed per terabyte of data processed, and queries files in the lake directly using OPENROWSET (or external tables). A dedicated SQL pool reserves and bills compute (DWUs) whether or not it is queried. A Spark pool uses notebooks and Spark, not pay-per-query T-SQL over files. Azure Analysis Services is a separate tabular modeling engine, not a lake query service.

questions.question: An Azure Data Factory pipeline must copy only rows inserted or changed since the previous run from a SQL source. Which approach implements this incremental load?
options: Always run a full copy and let the sink deduplicate
Store a high-watermark value (such as max LastModified) and copy only rows greater than the stored watermark
Use a tumbling window of one second on the source
Disable the staging area on the Copy activity
questions.explanation: The watermark pattern records the last processed value (such as the maximum LastModified or an incrementing key), then each run copies only rows greater than that stored value and updates the watermark afterward. A full copy every run is not incremental and wastes resources. Tumbling windows schedule pipeline runs but do not by themselves filter changed rows. The staging setting affects PolyBase/COPY staging, not change detection.

questions.question: In an Azure Stream Analytics job you must report the event count for each fixed, non-overlapping 30-second interval, with every event belonging to exactly one window. Which windowing function should you use?
options: Hopping window
Sliding window
Session window
Tumbling window
questions.explanation: A tumbling window divides time into fixed-length, contiguous, non-overlapping segments, so each event falls into exactly one window, which is ideal for counting events per 30 seconds. Hopping windows can overlap, so an event may appear in several. Sliding windows produce output as events enter or leave and overlap continuously. Session windows group bursts of activity separated by gaps, so their length varies.

questions.question: In Azure Databricks you must incrementally ingest new files as they land in a Data Lake Storage Gen2 folder, processing only files not seen before and without re-listing the entire directory each run. Which feature is designed for this?
options: Auto Loader (the cloudFiles source in Structured Streaming)
A static batch read with spark.read.parquet over the whole folder
The COPY INTO command run as a one-time full load
Manually deleting files after each successful read
questions.explanation: Auto Loader uses the cloudFiles source to incrementally and efficiently process new files as they arrive, tracking processed files through checkpoints (and optional file notifications) so it never reprocesses or fully re-lists the directory. A static spark.read reprocesses everything each run. A single COPY INTO is a one-time bulk load, not continuous incremental ingestion. Deleting source files is destructive and loses the raw data.

questions.question: Support staff must see customer email addresses with most characters hidden (for example aXXX@XXXX.com) while the underlying stored values stay unchanged and privileged roles still see full data. Which Azure SQL or Synapse feature provides this?
options: Transparent Data Encryption (TDE)
Always Encrypted
Dynamic Data Masking
Row-Level Security
questions.explanation: Dynamic Data Masking obfuscates data in query results for non-privileged users while leaving the stored values intact; members with the unmask permission still see full values. TDE encrypts data at rest on disk and is transparent to queries, so it does not mask results. Always Encrypted protects data end-to-end with client-side keys, hiding it even from admins, which is more than required. Row-Level Security filters which rows a user sees, not how column values are displayed.

questions.question: In a dedicated SQL pool, each regional manager must see only the sales rows for their own region, enforced automatically inside the database regardless of how the query is written. Which feature should you implement?
options: Column-level security
Row-Level Security using a security predicate function and a security policy
Dynamic Data Masking on the Region column
Granting SELECT on separate per-region views only
questions.explanation: Row-Level Security uses an inline table-valued predicate function bound to the table through a security policy, so the engine transparently filters rows (for example by region) for every query without changing application code. Column-level security restricts which columns, not which rows, are visible. Dynamic Data Masking only obscures displayed values. Per-region views can work but are not automatic, scale poorly, and are easy to bypass if base-table access is granted.

questions.question: An Azure Data Factory pipeline must authenticate to Azure Data Lake Storage Gen2 without storing any account keys, secrets, or connection strings in the linked service. What is the recommended approach?
options: Embed the storage account key directly in the linked service
Generate a long-lived SAS token and paste it into the pipeline
Store the account key in the pipeline parameters
Use the data factory's managed identity and grant it the Storage Blob Data Contributor role
questions.explanation: A system-assigned or user-assigned managed identity lets Data Factory authenticate to Storage through Microsoft Entra ID with no secrets in the configuration; you grant it an RBAC role such as Storage Blob Data Contributor on the account or container. Embedding the account key or storing it in parameters exposes a powerful long-lived secret. A long-lived SAS token is still a secret that must be rotated and can leak, so it is not the recommended secret-free option.

questions.question: An Azure Data Factory pipeline must copy data from a SQL Server instance that lives on a private corporate network with no public endpoint. What does the integration require?
options: A self-hosted integration runtime installed on a machine that can reach the SQL Server
The Azure integration runtime with the 'allow trusted Azure services' firewall exception enabled
An SSIS integration runtime provisioned in the same region as the Data Factory instance
A REST linked service pointed at the SQL Server's Tabular Data Stream endpoint over port 1433
questions.explanation: The self-hosted IR is the bridge to private networks: installed inside the network (or one reachable from it), it executes the copy and dispatches activities the Azure IR cannot reach. The Azure IR only reaches endpoints routable from Azure; the SSIS IR exists to run SSIS packages; REST linked services speak HTTP, not TDS.

questions.question: For bulk-loading Parquet files from ADLS Gen2 into a dedicated SQL pool table, which loading method does Microsoft now recommend for its combination of simplicity and throughput?
options: The bcp command-line utility running on a jumpbox with sixteen parallel client streams
The COPY INTO statement
Singleton INSERT statements batched in 1,000-row transactions from the application tier
Linked-server queries from an Azure SQL Database pulling the files through OPENROWSET
questions.explanation: COPY INTO is the recommended loader for dedicated SQL pools: a single T-SQL statement that reads directly from storage with high parallelism, simpler permissions than PolyBase external tables and far less setup than either. bcp and row-by-row INSERTs funnel data through the control node or client; linked servers aren't a Synapse loading path.

questions.question: A Customer dimension must preserve full history: when a customer's segment changes, the old row is kept and a new row becomes current. Which design implements this Type 2 slowly changing dimension?
options: Overwrite the segment column in place on the existing dimension row and rely on the storage account's nightly snapshots whenever historical questions need answering
Add a Segment_Previous column that always carries the value the attribute held before the latest update
Surrogate keys with effective-date and end-date (or current-flag) columns; updates close the old row and insert a new one
Partition the dimension table by calendar year so each year's rows reflect that year's attribute values
questions.explanation: SCD Type 2 keeps one row per version of the member: a surrogate key per version, validity dates or an is-current flag, with facts joining on the surrogate key valid at transaction time. Overwriting is Type 1 (history lost); a single 'previous' column is Type 3 (one step of history only); partitioning organizes storage, not attribute versioning.

questions.question: A Delta Lake table in Databricks was corrupted by a bad merge at 14:30. The team must query the table exactly as it was at 14:00 to validate and restore the data. Which capability do they use?
options: Delta time travel — querying the table with VERSION AS OF or TIMESTAMP AS OF
The storage account's geo-redundant secondary endpoint, which lags minutes behind the primary
Spark Structured Streaming's checkpoint directory replayed up to the 14:00 watermark offset
The vacuum command with a retention window of thirty minutes to roll back the bad files
questions.explanation: Delta's transaction log retains previous table versions, so `SELECT … TIMESTAMP AS OF '14:00'` (or RESTORE to that version) reads the pre-merge state directly. GRS secondaries aren't queryable point-in-time copies; streaming checkpoints track source offsets, not table state; VACUUM deletes old files — run carelessly it would destroy the very history needed.

questions.question: In Azure Stream Analytics, support-chat events for one visitor arrive in bursts; a 'conversation' should end when no event arrives for 5 minutes, however long the burst lasted. Which window type models this?
options: Tumbling window of five minutes aligned to the wall clock for each visitor partition
Hopping window of five minutes with a one-minute hop so burst boundaries are smoothed across the overlaps
Snapshot window grouping all events that share exactly the same arrival timestamp value
Session window with a five-minute timeout (and a maximum duration), partitioned by visitor
questions.explanation: Session windows grow while events keep arriving and close after the configured gap of inactivity — the natural model for conversations, user sessions and bursts of telemetry. Tumbling and hopping windows have fixed clock-driven boundaries that split conversations arbitrarily; snapshot windows group same-timestamp events only.

questions.question: A lakehouse follows the medallion architecture. What distinguishes the BRONZE layer from silver and gold?
options: Bronze stores aggregated, business-ready tables that analysts consume in BI dashboards
Bronze holds raw data as ingested from sources, kept with minimal transformation for replay and audit
Bronze contains the conformed, deduplicated entities shared by every downstream domain team
Bronze is the temporary staging area where source extracts are deleted immediately after each successful downstream load completes
questions.explanation: Bronze is the raw landing layer — source-shaped, append-oriented, preserving history so pipelines can be replayed and audited. Silver holds the cleaned, conformed, deduplicated entities; gold serves curated, aggregated business-level tables for consumption. Bronze data is deliberately retained, not deleted after load.

questions.question: A transformation step requires Python with scikit-learn over a few hundred gigabytes of Parquet, producing features written back to the lake. Which Synapse compute is the right tool?
options: A dedicated SQL pool, with the Python logic rewritten as T-SQL window functions and CASE expressions
A serverless SQL pool, since it can already read the Parquet files in place without any loading
An Apache Spark pool running the Python code as a notebook or Spark job over the files
The Data Factory copy activity with a mapping data flow expression implementing the model
questions.explanation: Spark pools execute Python (PySpark + libraries like scikit-learn) at scale directly over lake files — exactly the workload described. SQL pools execute T-SQL only: rewriting an ML featurization in T-SQL is impractical, and serverless SQL is a query engine, not a Python runtime. Mapping data flows offer visual transformations, not arbitrary Python.

questions.question: An ADF pipeline must run for every hourly slice of data, support automatic backfill of the last 90 days, retry failed slices individually, and allow slice N to depend on slice N-1. Which trigger type provides all of this?
options: A tumbling window trigger
A schedule trigger firing at minute zero of every hour in the factory's local time zone
A storage event trigger on the landing container filtered to blobs ending in .complete
A manual trigger invoked hourly by an Azure Automation runbook with a 90-day loop parameter
questions.explanation: Tumbling window triggers are stateful per-window: each hourly window is tracked individually, past windows backfill automatically from the start time, failed windows retry in isolation, and self-dependency chains window N on N-1. Schedule triggers are fire-and-forget with no window state; event triggers react to blobs, not time slices; a runbook reimplements all of it by hand.

questions.question: Telemetry from thousands of devices flows through Azure Event Hubs, and downstream processing requires that each individual device's events are consumed in the order they were sent. What ensures this?
options: Raising the Event Hubs throughput units so the service never needs to reorder under load
Setting the device ID as the partition key, since ordering is guaranteed within a partition
Enabling the Capture feature so events are also written to storage in arrival order
Publishing with AMQP instead of HTTPS, because AMQP provides global ordering across partitions
questions.explanation: Event Hubs guarantees order within a partition only; using the device ID as partition key routes each device's events to one partition, preserving per-device order while still scaling across partitions. Throughput units affect capacity, not ordering; Capture archives whatever order partitions had; no protocol provides cross-partition global ordering.

questions.question: The on-call engineer must be paged whenever any production ADF pipeline run fails, without anyone watching the monitoring UI. What is the Azure-native way to set this up?
options: Increase the activity retry count to ten so failures self-heal before anyone needs paging
Enable verbose logging on every activity and review the output files during business hours
Add an If Condition activity at the end of each production pipeline that sends an email to the team's shared mailbox whenever the preceding activity reports failure
An Azure Monitor metric alert on the 'Failed pipeline runs' metric, with an action group that pages the on-call
questions.explanation: Data Factory emits metrics to Azure Monitor; an alert rule on Failed pipeline runs tied to an action group (SMS, push, voice, webhook to PagerDuty/Opsgenie) pages the on-call automatically and covers every pipeline centrally. An If Condition only runs if the pipeline reaches it — many failures never do; retries and log reviews don't notify anyone.
